revision_brief: White male enlisted frontier gunner, 1874–1880, wearing a plain dark-blue short military sack coat, low dark forage cap, sky-blue straight trousers and black leather ankle boots. Distinct broad square face, reddish moustache, about forty. Stand at ease to the left of a realistically full-sized Model 1874 ten-barrel Gatling field gun, after the inspected Scientific American February 7, 1874 engraving: two large wooden spoked wheels with iron rims, a continuous axle, long wood-and-iron trail touching ground behind, clustered ten slender steel barrels in brass breech housing, manual hand crank and elevation support. Gun at waist/chest level; wheels approximately 1.35m diameter beside a 1.85m man. Feed drum removed as in the source engraving, no invented rectangular magazine. No tripod, no shield, no modern ammunition belt, no machine-gun motor. Figure and gun separate, entire wheel carriage and trailing support in frame; gun pointed sideways away from figure. Square composition, man left and gun right, full-sized equipment takes equal space. No horse or limber.

revision_brief: Distinct white male mounted frontier courier about thirty in the western United States in the 1880s. Slim athletic adult, long narrow face, clean-shaven, short sandy hair. Weathered tan broad-brim felt hat with plain low rounded crown; muted dusty blue straight-cut hip-length wool sack jacket open over ivory cotton shirt and russet waistcoat, small dark rust neckerchief; high-waisted brown straight trousers, calf-high brown leather riding boots and simple leather belt. Closed dark brown leather mail satchel with broad shoulder strap at left hip, no insignia or readable lettering. One small loop of spare plain leather rein at belt provides an equestrian cue. Neutral relaxed standing figure alone, dismounted; no horse, firearm, half-chaps, modern zippers, spurs or fantasy accessories. This is a fictional working rider, not an invented portrait of a named postal employee.
